Traditional sourdough is made with wheat or rye, so it isn't safe for your coeliac guest. I've built the plan around a **gluten-free sourdough** as the centrepiece instead.

## Centrepiece: gluten-free sourdough
- **Starter:** use a dedicated gluten-free starter (brown rice or sorghum flour and water). Never reuse a wheat starter, even a "cleaned" one.
- **Flour blend:** brown rice, sorghum, buckwheat or teff, plus tapioca or potato starch. Psyllium husk or xanthan gum gives structure.
- **Baking:** bake in a kitchen and on equipment with no wheat residue. Use new or thoroughly scrubbed tins, a clean oven, and no shared flour dust. Bake the day of the party, or the day before and reheat.
- **Serving:** slice with a dedicated bread knife and board, and put out separate butter and dips so crumbs from gluten-containing items don't get in.

## Menu
**Grazing and starters**
- Sourdough with whipped herb butter, olive tapenade, and hummus
- Cheese and charcuterie board (check the cured meats are gluten-free) with grapes and quince paste
- Gluten-free crackers or rice cakes as an alternative to the bread
- Crudités with tzatziki

**Mains**
- Slow-roast chicken thighs with lemon and thyme, seasoned with salt, pepper, and herbs only
- Roasted vegetable and quinoa salad
- Potato salad with a homemade vinaigrette

**Dessert**
- Flourless chocolate cake (made with almond meal)
- Fresh fruit platter with whipped cream

## Gluten checks
- Read the labels on stock, sauces, mustard, dressings, and cured meats.
- Use tamari labelled gluten-free instead of regular soy sauce.
- Keep gluten-free items separate on the table, ideally with serving utensils for each dish.

Tell me the number of guests, any other dietary needs, and whether you're baking yourself or using a caterer, and I'll turn this into a shopping list and a baking timeline.
